1.sense: The hypocrites come to the Prophet ﷺ and say the correct words: they testify that he is the messenger of Allah. The verse does not dispute the sentence, since Allah already knows it is true; it disputes the men who say it. The closing clause turns their own verb, bear witness, back on them, so that what Allah testifies to is not the truth of their statement but the falseness of their saying it.

notes.t: The verse frames their testimony between two mentions of Allah knowing and Allah witnessing, so the shahada is true as a sentence and false as an act: the words match what a believer says, the heart behind them does not.
The claim to believe without believing opens the description of hypocrisy in Al-Baqarah: people who say they believe in Allah and the Last Day but are not believers.

Zayd ibn Arqam reported to the Prophet ﷺ what he had heard Abdullah ibn Ubayy say against him on the campaign; Abdullah denied it under oath, and this surah was revealed confirming Zayd's report. It is carried in Bukhari and Muslim.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Zayd ibn Arqam

links.why: the same shape of claim, believing named in words that the following verses show are not matched by the heart

2.sense: Their oaths are not offered as evidence of sincerity; they are used as cover. The same swearing that would seem to prove faith is turned here into a screen that keeps the hypocrites from suspicion while they act against Allah's way. The verse closes on a plain judgment of the pattern of their conduct, not a single act.

notes.t: Junnah is a shield carried in battle; the image casts oath-taking as a defensive tactic rather than a devotional act, something raised to block a blow rather than spoken in sincerity.
The same phrase, they have taken their oaths as a shield and turned away from the way of Allah, is used almost word for word of another group in Al-Mujadila.

links.why: the identical opening phrase applied to a different group, showing the charge is a recurring pattern rather than a one-time accusation

3.sense: The verse gives the reason for the sealing named here: belief came first and disbelief followed it, a profession discarded rather than one never made. What is closed off is understanding, not information, they can still speak the creed, as the first verse showed, while missing what it means.

notes.t: Fiqh is understanding that reaches into a matter, not bare awareness of facts; the sealing blocks comprehension rather than speech, which is why the same men can recite the shahada correctly in the opening verse.
The same image of a seal placed on the heart opens the description of the disbelievers at the start of the Qur'an.

Exegetes read believed then disbelieved two ways: an inward faith later abandoned, or an outward profession of Islam spoken without the conviction that would have made it real belief in the first place. The two readings are not resolved against each other.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record both readings

links.why: the same image of a seal placed on the heart, in the opening description of disbelief
reverting to disbelief after guidance had already become clear, the same sequence named here

4.sense: Two separate signs are named and then undercut: their appearance draws the eye and their speech draws the ear, and neither carries the substance a body or a statement should carry. The simile compares them to timbers leaned against a wall, upright and shaped but hollow, standing without bearing any weight. Their fear runs the same way, every shout in the camp, they take as aimed at them, because the guilt sits under the surface they present.

notes.t: Musannadatun describes wood propped against something rather than built into it; it stands but supports nothing, matching men whose outward form carries no inner substance behind it.
The verse's closing words, may He fight them, how are they deluded, repeat the exact curse formula used of those who exaggerated their religious leaders in Surah at-Tawbah.

links.why: speech that pleases the listener while hiding the fiercest enmity in the speaker's heart
the identical closing curse, may Allah fight them, how are they deluded

5.sense: The offer is stated plainly: come, and the Prophet ﷺ will ask forgiveness for you. The refusal is physical before it is spoken, a twist of the head away from the one speaking. The fault named at the end is not shame or indifference but arrogance, the specific defect that keeps a person from asking to be forgiven at all.

notes.t: Twisting the head away is a bodily gesture of contempt rather than a spoken answer; the verse records their rejection before any word of theirs is quoted.
The same scene, an appeal made and hypocrites turning away in aversion, is described in Surah an-Nisa using the same verb for turning away.

links.why: the same refusal, hypocrites turning away when called to the Prophet ﷺ, using the same verb

6.sense: The offer named in the previous verse is closed from the other side: the Prophet's ﷺ intercession is not withheld by his own choice but made ineffective by a condition in them. Setting the two options, asking or not asking, as equal states that no act of supplication changes an outcome resting on something else, their persistence in fisq, open defiance of a command they already know.

notes.t: The same statement, that it makes no difference whether the Prophet ﷺ asks forgiveness for them, is made of the same period and the same men in Surah at-Tawbah.
Fisq names a specific fault, stepping outside a boundary once inside it, distinct from kufr, never having entered: the same shape as belief held and then abandoned in the third verse of this surah.
Even Ibrahim's asking forgiveness for his father was withdrawn once it became clear he was an enemy of Allah, setting a limit on intercession that this verse states directly for the hypocrites.

links.why: the same statement made of the same men after Abdullah ibn Ubayy's death

7.sense: A specific tactic is quoted directly: cut off support from the people around the Prophet ﷺ so that they scatter for lack of means. The reply is not an appeal to generosity but a statement of ownership, the treasuries of the heavens and the earth already belong to Allah, so withholding support was never going to starve anyone out on its own terms. The verse repeats the charge of not understanding, made earlier in the surah of the same men.

notes.t: Khaza'in, treasuries, names stores kept in reserve; naming Allah's is the direct answer to a plan built on cutting off supply, since the supply was never in the hypocrites' hands to withhold.
Not to think withholding what Allah has given is good for the one withholding it is stated as a general rule about wealth in Al Imran.

links.why: the same misjudgment, that withholding wealth from Allah's cause serves the one who withholds it

8.sense: The verse quotes their private boast about the balance of power in Madinah, naming themselves the mighty and the Prophet's ﷺ followers the weak. The reply corrects the term itself: 'izzah, might, belongs to Allah, and through Him to His messenger and the believers, so the boast has claimed a word that was never theirs to give out. The closing fault is knowledge rather than the understanding named twice already, since what fails here is a reading of where power actually sits.

notes.t: The saying is reported from Abdullah ibn Ubayy on the campaign against Banu al-Mustaliq. Zayd ibn Arqam heard him say it and told the Prophet ﷺ; Abdullah denied it under oath, and this surah was revealed affirming Zayd. It is carried in Bukhari and Muslim.
notes.src: Bukhari and Muslim, from Zayd ibn Arqam

notes.t: Mighty and weak are a paired opposite running through the verse, and the reply keeps the same pair but reassigns it, since might turns out to be something given rather than something seized by a faction.
Seeking honor through disbelievers is corrected the same way in an-Nisa: all honor belongs to Allah entirely.

links.why: the same correction, that honor sought anywhere but through Allah is misdirected

9.sense: The address shifts from the hypocrites to the believers, and the danger named is distraction rather than disbelief. Wealth and children are not called wrong in themselves; the fault is letting either pull attention away from remembering Allah. The verse ends on a plain label, loss, without describing what is lost or how.

notes.t: The verb describes distraction as something wealth and children do to a person over time, an ongoing pull rather than a single choice made once and finished.
Wealth and children named together as a trial, with a great reward held with Allah instead, opens the same pairing in Al-Anfal.
The same pairing of wealth and children as a trial, and the same reward held with Allah, is repeated in the surah that immediately follows this one.

links.why: the same pairing named as a trial rather than a good or an evil in itself
the nearly identical line in the following surah, at-Taghabun

10.sense: The command returns to the address of the previous verse: spend from what you were given, before death removes the choice. What follows is the plea of someone too late, asking for a short postponement to do the one thing, give charity, that would have needed no death-bed request had it been done earlier. The wish names its own ordinary size, not a long new life, just a near term.

notes.t: Fa-assaddaqa carries an intensified verb form for what is grammatically a plain future action, which grammarians read as marking a wish spoken with unusual force: the strongest form of the verb for the smallest, latest request.

Spend from what We have provided you before a day comes opens an almost identical command in Al-Baqarah, there naming a day with no exchange, friendship, or intercession instead of a person's own death.
The same death-bed plea for a return, phrased as my Lord, send me back, so that I may act righteously in what I left behind, is described and refused in Al-Mu'minun.

links.why: the identical opening command to spend from what Allah provided before it is too late
the same too-late plea, generalized there to every good deed left undone rather than charity alone

11.sense: The plea just quoted is answered as the surah closes: the request for reprieve is refused as a rule, not only in that one case. The verb here, delay, is the same word the dying person used to ask for reprieve in the verse before, so the refusal is built from the very word of the request. The final clause turns from what is fixed, the length of a life, to what is not, the record of what was done with it.

notes.t: Yu'akhkhira here and akhkhartani in the verse before share the same root, so the refusal directly negates the specific word just used in the plea for more time.
That a term, once it comes, cannot be delayed or advanced by an hour is stated of nations rather than individuals in Surah al-A'raf.

links.why: the same rule applied to the term of a nation rather than a single soul
the same closing formula, the term of Allah, when it comes, is not delayed

1.sense: The surah opens with everything in the heavens and earth already engaged in glorifying Allah, before any command is given to a human listener. Dominion and praise both belong to him without division, and the final clause states the ground for both: power over everything.

notes.t: Five surahs open with this glorification formula: Al-Hadid, Al-Hashr, As-Saff, Al-Jumuʿa, and this one. Al-Hadid, Al-Hashr, and As-Saff use the past tense sabbaha; this surah and Al-Jumuʿa use the present tense yusabbihu, an ongoing act rather than a completed one.
The pairing of universal dominion with power over everything closes the fifth surah as well, in almost the same words.

links.why: the same present-tense opening, yusabbihu, in the surah just before this one
the same claim in the same order: dominion, then power over all things

2.sense: Creation is one act, but it does not produce one outcome. Some of those he made turn out disbelieving, some believing, and the verse states this split as a plain fact before saying anything about which is chosen. What follows is not a verdict but a notice: Allah watches what each of them does with it.

notes.t: The verse does not explain why creation yields both outcomes; it states the split and moves straight to Allah's watching, leaving the reason for another verse and another argument.
The same choice is put directly to the listener: whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.

links.why: the same fork stated as an open choice rather than an observed fact
the guidance given to every person, to be met with either gratitude or ingratitude

3.sense: Bi-l-haqq, in truth, marks the heavens and earth as made with purpose rather than left to stand for no reason. The same sentence moves from that scale down to the individual body: shaped, and shaped well. Both endpoints, the vast and the personal, run back to the same return.

notes.t: Bi-l-haqq recurs across the Qur'an as the standing answer to the idea that the world was made idly; here it sits beside a second claim, that the human form itself was made well, joining cosmic and personal design in one verse.
The heavens and the earth and what is between them were not created as a plaything, and not left without purpose.

links.why: the same claim about the heavens and earth, made at greater length
man made in the best of forms, the same claim this verse makes about ṣuwarakum

4.sense: Knowledge is traced through three widening circles: everything in the heavens and earth, then what people hide or say aloud, then the breast itself, the seat where an intention forms before it becomes speech or an act. Nothing in that sequence sits outside it.

notes.t: "What is in the breasts" is the Qur'an's standing idiom for intention at its source, prior to speech: not the mind in the abstract but the chest as the felt location of what a person means.
The same phrase closes a verse on concealed and open speech: whether you keep your word secret or state it aloud, he knows what is in the breasts.

links.why: the identical closing phrase, applied there to speech kept secret or spoken aloud

5.sense: The question assumes an answer: the report of earlier disbelieving peoples has reached its audience, whether or not they have taken it in. Those peoples already tasted the bad outcome of their own conduct in this world. A further, painful punishment is named as still owed beyond that.

notes.t: "Tasted" treats the ruin of earlier nations as something already experienced and finished, distinct from the punishment still described as future and painful in the same verse.
The same rhetorical question opens a passage naming specific ruined nations, Noah's people, 'Ad, and Thamud, as the news being asked about.

links.why: the same question, with the earlier peoples named directly

6.sense: The punishment in the prior verse is traced to a cause: their own messengers kept bringing them clear proofs, and their answer was a question meant to close the matter, shall a mere human being guide us. They disbelieved and turned away on that basis. Allah had no need of their belief; the verse says so twice, once as something that happened and once as a standing description of him.

notes.t: "Abasharun yahdunana" treats the messenger's humanity itself as the objection, as if guidance could only be credible coming from something other than a man.
The same complaint is named as the one thing that ever stopped people from believing: that Allah sent a human being as a messenger.

links.why: the same objection stated as the single obstacle to belief

7.sense: The disbelievers' claim is stated first, flatly, then answered with an instruction rather than an argument: the Prophet ﷺ is told to swear to the opposite. Raised, then told everything done, and the verse closes by naming that as easy for Allah, not as something requiring proof of capacity.

notes.t: Balā, "yes indeed," is the fixed answer the Qur'an gives to a denial phrased as a negative oath; the reply corrects the claim in the same breath it is made.
The same denial and the same answer appear together: they swore by Allah that he would not raise the dead, yes indeed, a true promise binding on him.

links.why: the same oath of denial met with the same word, balā

8.sense: The instruction follows directly from the case just made: believe in Allah, in his messenger, and in the light sent down through him. Light is the Qur'an's own name here for what was revealed, not a separate object of belief alongside it. The verse ends where it keeps ending in this surah, on Allah's awareness of conduct.

notes.t: "An-nur" for revelation names light as something that shows what was otherwise hidden, paired here with belief in the messenger who carried it rather than treated as a fourth, independent article.
Revelation is named the same way elsewhere: a light and a clear book has come to you from Allah.

links.why: the same pairing of light and revelation from Allah

9.sense: This names the day the surah is titled after: the day of gathering, called here the day of taghābun, mutual loss and gain, a term from trade for the moment one side in a deal discovers what the other has walked away with. Belief paired with right action earns two things at once, bad deeds removed and entry into gardens with rivers running beneath, permanently. The verse calls that the great triumph.

notes.t: Taghābun comes from ghabn, being cheated or shortchanged in a bargain; on this day each side sees plainly what it gained and what it gave up, which is why the Day of Judgment is named for a transaction rather than a trial.
The same reward is described in almost the same words: I will remove their bad deeds and admit them to gardens beneath which rivers flow.

links.why: the same promise, sins removed and gardens entered, in near-identical wording

10.sense: The other half of the same day: those who disbelieved and called Allah's signs false are named companions of the fire, remaining there. Where the prior verse held two outcomes together, gain and its cost, this side of the ledger holds only loss, and the verse says so in its last word.

notes.t: "Companions of the fire" pairs directly against the entry into gardens just given, the two verses forming one balanced statement of the day's two outcomes.
The same sentence closes a passage in the second surah almost word for word: those who disbelieved and denied our signs, those are companions of the fire, abiding therein.

links.why: nearly the same sentence, closing a different surah's opening passage

11.sense: No affliction lands outside Allah's permission; the calamity itself is placed inside his decree rather than treated as something that happens to him as well as to the person it strikes. Belief is answered in kind, a guided heart, and the verse closes on knowledge that covers everything, the affliction included.

notes.t: The verse does not say what "guides his heart" produces in the moment of loss; it states the guidance as the believer's due, alongside the affliction, not as its removal.
The same claim is put in the first person as something to say: nothing will befall us except what Allah has decreed for us.

links.why: the same claim about decree, given as words to say when calamity comes

12.sense: The command to obey is given twice, once for Allah and once for the messenger, rather than folded into a single verb. If the audience turns away anyway, the messenger's task was never to force their response; it was to deliver the message clearly, and that much has been done regardless of what they do with it.

notes.t: Repeating atīʿū rather than writing it once keeps obedience to the messenger a distinct act, not a claim absorbed into obedience to Allah.
The closing clause repeats an earlier verse almost word for word: if you turn away, then know that our messenger's duty is only clear delivery.

links.why: the same closing sentence, near verbatim, in an earlier surah

13.sense: The declaration of exclusive oneness is stated plainly, with no argument attached to it here. What follows is not further description but an instruction drawn straight from it: since there is no other, let the believers place their reliance on Allah alone.

notes.t: Lā ilāha illā huwa functions as a hinge in this verse: the whole instruction to rely on Allah is given as a direct consequence of it, joined by no more than "and."
The same declaration opens a passage in almost the same words: Allah, there is no god but him, the ever-living, the sustainer.

links.why: the same declaration used to open a different passage

14.sense: Believers are told that an enemy to their commitment can sit inside their own household, among spouses and children rather than outside it. The instruction is caution, not separation: the same sentence turns at once to pardon, overlooking, and forgiveness as the better response, and pairs that choice with Allah's own forgiveness and mercy.

notes.t: ʿAduwwan is singular though the household named is plural, naming the pull itself as a single enemy rather than accusing any one family member by name.
The surah immediately before this one gives the same warning in nearly the same words: let not your wealth and your children divert you from remembrance of Allah.

links.why: the adjacent surah's version of the same warning about wealth and children

15.sense: The same pair, wealth and children, is named again, now generalized past the one household enemy of the prior verse into a trial as such: something that tests where loyalty and priority actually sit. Set against it is what Allah holds in reserve, called a greater reward.

notes.t: Fitnah carries the sense of testing by fire, the process that shows what a metal is made of, closer to trial than to simple temptation.
The same sentence appears earlier in the Qur'an almost word for word: know that your wealth and your children are a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward.

links.why: the same sentence, nearly verbatim, earlier in the Qur'an

16.sense: The standard is explicitly scaled to what a person can do, then widened outward into listening, obeying, and spending, with the spending named as a good done for the giver rather than a loss to him. Success at the end is tied to one specific guard: being kept from the stinginess native to one's own soul.

notes.t: Shuḥḥ, an ingrained stinginess of the self, is a different word from bukhl, a miserly act: the trait rather than a single instance of withholding.

Some exegetes read this clause, be mindful of Allah as much as you are able, as easing the stricter standard given earlier, fear Allah as he should be feared, though others treat the two as simply consistent rather than one relaxing the other.
notes.src: discussed in Ibn Kathīr's tafsīr on this verse, against 3:102

notes.t: The closing clause repeats an earlier verse word for word: whoever is guarded against the stinginess of his own soul, those are the successful.

links.why: the stricter standard this verse's wording is often read against
the identical closing clause, said there of the Anṣār

17.sense: Spending is cast here as a loan given to Allah himself, a good loan, meaning one given without expectation of worldly return. What comes back is doubled and paired with forgiveness. The two closing names fit the transaction: appreciative of what is given, forbearing toward what is held back.

notes.t: Naming voluntary spending a loan to Allah reframes it as a transaction with a guaranteed return rather than a gift with none, dignifying the giver's side of it.
The same offer is put as a question elsewhere: who will lend Allah a good loan, that he may multiply it for him many times over.

links.why: the same loan put as a direct question, with the multiplication spelled out

18.sense: The surah closes on four names set side by side with no verb joining them: knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the mighty, the wise. The first pair states the reach of his knowledge; the second states the reach of his power and his judgment.

notes.t: Al-ghayb and ash-shahādah together form a merism, two opposites standing for the whole: what is hidden and what is present cover all there is to know, leaving nothing outside either half.
The same pairing of names closes a passage naming Allah's attributes at length: he is Allah, there is no god but him, knower of the unseen and the witnessed.

links.why: the same pairing, knower of the unseen and the witnessed, in a longer list of names
